newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rupee strength bucks regional trend.
newsitem.headline: Indian rupee strength bucks regional trend.

text.p: The Indian rupee is bursting with strength, undaunted by either the dollar's supremacy against other major currencies or a domino-effect collapse among south-east Asian currencies, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday.
Waves of portfolio investment have poured into Asia's best-performing stock market in 1997.

The Bombay stock index is up almost 30 percent from January 1, striking 33-month highs last week, and because of the rupee's strength the profile looks even stronger. There has also been a regular stream of foreign direct investment (FDI).
"The reason the rupee's been so strong is the steady inflow of foreign funds and weak import demand," said Nupur Joshi, economist at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking Ltd.
"And the central bank has not been intervening as actively as it can."

While other central banks around south and south-east Asia are either actively devaluing or battling against tumbling currencies, the Reserve Bank of India has struggled to keep the rupee on a tight rein.
The RBI, along with India's largest state-owned commercial bank, State Bank of India, dominates India's currency market.
But the cost of intervening is causing a growing problem for the RBI, which has to neutralise the growth in money supply caused by selling rupees for dollars.
India's foreign currency reserves totalled $25.4 billion in June, compared with $17.3 billion a year ago.

Portfolio investment inflows and FDI amounted to $5.0 billion in 1996/97 (April-March). And since April portfolio investment inflows have totaled around $700 million. There are no reliable figures for FDI inflows this fiscal year.
Add to this the herd of Indian corporates raising foreign currency loans abroad. The flood of money coming in will test the RBI's ability to contain the rupee for much longer.
About $50 billion is traded in rupee-dollar transactions each month, according to RBI estimates.
The power of inflows is likely to get greater as India moves towards a capital account convertibility. The rupee is presently convertible on the current account.

An unexpected absence of RBI intervention allowed the rupee to break below 35.70 to the dollar on Friday, marking its strongest level for seven months. It finished Tuesday around 35.71, after the RBI came in again to sell rupees.

On its real effective exchange rate (REER) the rupee has appreciated by around seven percent in the last 12 months, analysts said. The RBI does not publish its REER index on a daily basis, so uptodate, precise calculations are difficult.
India's rung further down the development ladder puts the rupee in a different cycle from south-east Asian currencies.
"India is an emerging market, not an Asian market," said Mark McFarland, economist at Peregrine Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong.

South East Asian countries are well established on their development paths, while India is coming from a lot further back, analysts said. Liberal economic reforms began in India in 1991, but have regained impetus in the last year under the stewardship of Finance Minister P.Chidamabaram.

"India is different because it is just liberalising. The inflows of foreign capital are linked to the changes in policy it is nothing to do with arbitraging interest rates or anything like that," Mcfarland said.

That drive towards reform have put India further along the track than its South Asian competitors, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. All three countries currencies have weakened either through pegged devaluations or slowly guided depreciation.
The currency divergence with its neighbours will hit India's exports, which are, software sector apart, low value added and price sensitive, analysts said.
Ravi Kumar, chief dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank in Bombay said a strong rupee to pay for capital imports and to build the home market made abundant sense, even if the export sector suffered.
